title: "Predetermined Chow test at 2011"
---

```{r}
#| label: setup

```

## Motivation

If the regime transition between supply-constrained (pre-2011) and demand-driven (post-2011) Bangladesh is the structural cause of the wave-by-wave sign flip, the transition should show up as a structural break in the C-section trajectory itself. The standard tool for this is the Chow test [@chow1960test].

A naïve Bai-Perron supF test for an *unknown* breakdate is not appropriate here: the asymptotic theory needs T much larger than the T = 6 DHS waves available. The predetermined Chow test — where the candidate breakdate is fixed *ex ante* from external information rather than searched in the data — has the standard F-distribution and is appropriate at small T.

The candidate breakdate is 2011, justified externally by:

- The WHO 15% threshold crossing in 2010 [@who2015csection]
- The acceleration of private-sector dominance [@sujon2025cesarean]
- The shift in the wealth gradient documented in Chapter 4

Importantly, the predetermined character of the test means the resulting F-statistic, even if not statistically significant at small T, is honest evidence: the breakdate was not chosen to maximize the statistic.

## Data and setup

Implementation: `scripts/50_phase_d_modern/54_chow_descriptive_break.R`. Bangladesh's wave-level rate from `P1_Csec_Trends_All.csv` (T = 6 waves: 2004, 2007, 2011, 2014, 2017.5, 2022) is fit to a pooled linear model and to a split model with an interaction at 2011; the Chow F-test compares the two.

## Results

```{r}
#| label: tbl-chow
#| tbl-cap: "Predetermined Chow test at 2011, Bangladesh C-section trajectory. Despite T = 6, the predetermined-breakdate test is significant at α = 0.01."
ch <- load_chow()
ch |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    Test = test,
    `F` = sprintf("%.2f", F_stat),
    df = sprintf("(%d, %d)", df1, df2),
    `p` = fmt_p(p_value),
    `Pre-2011 slope` = sprintf("%.3f", pre_2011_slope),
    `Post-2011 slope delta` = sprintf("%.3f", post_2011_slope_diff)
  ) |>
  book_table()
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-chow
#| fig-cap: "Bangladesh C-section trajectory with predetermined Chow break at 2011. WHO 15% threshold (green dotted) crossed in 2010; the slope discontinuity at 2011 (pre-2011 = 1.48 pp/year vs post-2011 ≈ 2.46 pp/year) is visually unambiguous."
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figures", "phase_d", "chow_descriptive_break.png"))
```

## Interpretation

The Chow F-statistic is large (≈ 246) with a p-value of ≈ 0.004. Despite T = 6 — which would normally produce wide CIs and a weak test — the break is so dramatic that the test rejects the no-break null at α = 0.01.

The substantive reading: Bangladesh's C-section trajectory is not a single linear process across 2004–2022. The pre-2011 era and the post-2011 era are statistically distinguishable phases. An IV identification strategy that assumes a *single* underlying selection mechanism across both phases — which is what the RBVP in Chapter 7 does — cannot be expected to recover a stable causal estimate.

This chapter closes the diagnostic chain. Chapters 6–14 documented three independent rejections of the bivariate probit's identifying assumptions; Chapter 15 documents the structural reason. The combination is conclusive: the wave-by-wave sign flip is real, the regime transition is real, the headline 2022 RBVP estimate is fragile under every modern sensitivity diagnostic, and the field needs a different design.
